title: IRAQ'S CASE — THE WAR THEY WOULD NOT END | IRAQI PERSPECTIVE CUT
editorial: A historically Iraqi-centered reading of two commissioned threads. Attributions are preserved for contested claims; original source links in collection.json, never displayed in the final video.

chapters.title: THE WAR BEFORE THE WAR
chapters.text: September twenty-second, nineteen eighty. The invasion is remembered. But from Baghdad, the story began before a single Iraqi aircraft crossed the frontier. It began with a revolution next door, a diplomatic opening, and an increasingly dangerous struggle over Iraq's security.

chapters.title: REVOLUTION AT IRAQ'S BORDER
chapters.text:
In nineteen seventy-nine, Iraq did not initially greet the new Islamic Republic as an enemy to be destroyed. An April telegram welcomed the change of government. Iraqi leaders then pursued contact with Tehran. Even the meeting portrayed here between Saddam Hussein and Ebrahim Yazdi belongs to that early attempt to keep relations open.

Yet the atmosphere around Iraq was changing. Revolutionary demonstrations, attacks on Iraqi diplomatic premises, and fierce ideological language became central to Baghdad's fears. The material places those tensions beside Saddam Hussein's warnings against support for separatist movements inside Iraq. Khomeini's response, as represented in the recordings, intensified the dispute over Arab unity and revolutionary authority.

For the Iraqi leadership, this was not simply a quarrel of personalities. It was the possibility that a revolution in a neighbouring state might be exported across Iraq's borders. That fear formed the core of Baghdad's political argument.

Then came the violence of nineteen eighty: the attack at Mustansiriya University and the attempted assassination of Tariq Aziz. The source material attributes wider attacks to Iranian-backed Dawa networks. Such responsibility is a serious allegation requiring more than an edited excerpt; the attempt and the escalating crisis nonetheless occupy a decisive place in the Iraqi account.

The result was a relationship moving away from diplomacy and toward confrontation. The point is not that every Iraqi accusation is thereby proven. It is that the political crisis did not suddenly emerge on September twenty-second.

chapters.title: THE BORDER UNDER FIRE
chapters.text:
The frontier itself now became the focus. The material assembles a long list of alleged airspace incursions, ground violations and artillery attacks. Iraqi complaints identify Khanaqin and Mandali, and describe shelling in early September nineteen eighty. These accusations deserve examination in their original language, not dismissal because they preceded the invasion.

The dispute was also legal and geographical. Under the nineteen seventy-five Algiers Agreement, Iraq and Iran had attempted to settle their frontier. By September nineteen eighty, each government disputed the other's conduct. Iraqi accounts say that Tehran rejected obligations, challenged positions along the border and obstructed navigation in the Shatt al Arab.

On September seventeenth Saddam Hussein declared the agreement void. That was an unmistakable political escalation. Days later the conflict passed from border fighting into a full-scale Iraqi invasion of Iran. The invasion happened; Baghdad's argument is that it occurred after a mounting series of provocations and failed attempts to resolve them.

chapters.title: THE ROAD NOT TAKEN
chapters.text:
What did Baghdad say it wanted once the war had begun? Here the Iraqi account makes one of its strongest claims: Iraq did not seek to conquer Iran, but to compel negotiations and secure its frontier. Saddam Hussein's recorded statements are used to support that position. A government's declared objective is not the same as independent proof of all its intentions. It is still essential evidence of the case that Baghdad made.

The Security Council adopted Resolution four hundred and seventy-nine only six days after the invasion. The material contrasts Iraq's willingness to accept an early cessation of hostilities with Tehran's rejection of the conditions offered at the time.

Iranian officials also discussed the cost of continued war. In the supplied testimony, the former Iranian general Masoud Bakhtiari and statements attributed to Iranian leaders are used to argue that opportunities for a ceasefire were missed.

Then comes a crucial shift. By nineteen eighty-two, Iran had recovered much of the territory lost in the invasion. The question was no longer only how to repel an occupying army, but why fighting should continue after that recovery.

The source argument is uncompromising: Iraq made diplomatic openings, and Khomeini's leadership chose to continue. The terms of each offer still matter. But the political decision to prolong the conflict is a central historical question, and not an afterthought.

chapters.title: THE INCIDENT DOSSIER
chapters.text:
Return to the pages on screen. Here the record is no longer a single speech or a single headline, but a sequence of alleged incidents before the war: aircraft crossing a frontier, artillery fired near towns, and ground confrontations across disputed positions.

The Iraqi argument draws force from the accumulation. The supplied material lists dozens of aerial and ground episodes between June and September nineteen eighty. These are reproduced allegations, not a complete independent finding on every entry. But they make the chronology impossible to reduce to one isolated event.

The historical issue is not whether a list can replace investigation. It cannot. The issue is whether the months before the invasion are treated as part of the war's origins. To present Iraq's experience from Baghdad, those months belong at the centre of the story.

chapters.title: BAGHDAD'S CASE FOR PEACE
chapters.text:
Listen to Baghdad's own case. In the attached speech, Saddam Hussein speaks of withdrawal and a ceasefire. The Iraqi position was that military pressure had a limited purpose and that negotiations should follow. Its defenders also point to later decisions not to annex occupied Iranian territory.

This is the argument often lost when the history begins and ends with the first invasion. Iraqi leaders wanted their security claims heard, and the available statements show how they presented them. Whether each proposal was unconditional, or acceptable to Tehran, requires the actual terms. But these declarations cannot simply be erased from the story.

chapters.title: THE FOREIGN ARMS NETWORK
chapters.text:
The second half of the case looks beyond the frontier. Foreign powers did not stand outside this conflict. The reproduced documents describe Israeli weapons transfers, American authorization questions and intermediaries supplying Iran.

Consider the contradiction that drives the argument. Iran's revolutionary leadership denounced Western influence. Yet the material describes channels through which Western and Israeli weapons reached the Islamic Republic. Some passages refer to high-level approval; others point to committees and covert procurement. Each record has its own evidentiary limits, but together they raise a serious question about the distance between public ideology and wartime practice.

From the Iraqi perspective, these transfers mattered because they helped keep Iran supplied while the fighting continued. The conflict was fought by Iraqis and Iranians, but outside interests could influence how long it lasted.

chapters.title: SUPPLYING TEHRAN
chapters.text:
The argument becomes more specific. Some reproduced pages concern satellite imagery and intelligence allegedly shared with Iran. Others discuss weapons supplied through Israel, procurement intermediaries and American contacts.

The passages do not all establish the same thing. A book's report of a transfer, a legislative document discussing HAWK missiles and a historian's estimate of foreign suppliers are different kinds of evidence. They must remain distinct. Yet the Iraqi reading of them is coherent: the Iranian war effort was not sustained by revolutionary determination alone.

Look especially at the congressional text reproduced here. It discusses assistance without a prior presidential finding, while leaving a question about presidential knowledge or consent unresolved. That nuance matters because accuracy makes the larger question stronger.

The material also names Soviet supplies, demonstrating that wartime procurement crossed supposed ideological lines. An Iraq facing its neighbour was also confronting the consequences of an international arms market. The Iraqi perspective asks who benefited when that war did not end quickly.

chapters.title: THE INTERNATIONAL CALCULATION
chapters.text:
Now listen to the strategic calculation attributed to Israeli intelligence officer Aharon Yariv: an outright Iraqi victory was not in Israel's interest. The source uses that assessment to connect weapons deliveries with a wider regional balance of power.

One cited estimate speaks of at least forty-one countries supplying Iran. The exact scope of the number needs its original context. What matters here is the argument that the war's supply networks were broader than the public political slogans suggested.

Iraq also faced the economic price of fighting. Wartime debts accumulated, while the military and families of the dead required continued support. The source interprets foreign discomfort with Iraqi strength after nineteen eighty-eight as part of the same strategic rivalry. That is a political reading, not proof of a single coordinated conspiracy. Yet the question of who welcomed an Iraqi victory is legitimate.

chapters.title: 1988 — IRAQ REGAINS THE INITIATIVE
chapters.text:
And then the battlefield changed. During the middle years of the war, the Iraqi army rebuilt its methods, organization and operational confidence. The material highlights the Tawakkalna ala Allah offensives as evidence of that transformation.

By nineteen eighty-eight, Iraqi forces were winning back positions that Iran had spent years trying to hold. The recovery of al Faw became a symbol of the shift. Further operations put Iranian forces under enormous pressure, while the war's financial and human burden mounted across Iran.

Here the sources introduce an Iranian veteran's retrospective account of how quickly positions were lost. The value of the recording lies in hearing a participant describe defeat from the other side of the battlefield; the exact figures attributed to him require confirmation from the complete statement.

For Iraq, these were not abstract movements of lines on a map. They were the recovery of ground, the preservation of the state, and the military culmination of years of fighting.

This is the centre of the Iraqi victory thesis. It does not require pretending that the war had been painless or that Iraq had never invaded Iran. It asks what the armies could achieve in the final campaign, and why Iran accepted a ceasefire after the military balance had shifted so sharply.

The final Iraqi offensives belong in the conclusion of the war, not in a footnote.

chapters.title: WHAT DOES VICTORY MEAN?
chapters.text:
The closing historical debate is not merely about where the border stood when the guns fell silent. Some of the authors reproduced here describe the military outcome as a decisive Iraqi victory. Stephen Pelletiere's analysis is central to that interpretation: the ability of Iraq's forces to recover territory and impose severe reverses on Iran, followed by Tehran's acceptance of a ceasefire.

Other reproduced passages challenge the idea that the war was simply an indecisive draw. Those are interpretations by identifiable authors; their existence does not make them a unanimous verdict.

But from Baghdad, military recovery in nineteen eighty-eight matters. A final outcome should account for the last offensives, the political decisions that followed, and the difference between an unchanged international border and an unchanged military balance. To call the war a stalemate without examining those final months leaves out the very evidence on which Iraq's case rests.

chapters.title: THE WAR THEY WOULD NOT END
chapters.text:
The war ended, but Iraq's predicament did not. The material closes with American concern about Iraqi power and the possibility of sanctions. A proposed measure is not proof that it became law, nor proof of one hidden motive.

The Iraqi case remains clear in its own terms: the conflict had a history before September nineteen eighty; Baghdad made diplomatic arguments that deserve scrutiny; foreign weapons reached Tehran; and Iraq regained the military initiative in nineteen eighty-eight.

Those are the questions this film places on the record. The images are real reproductions. The judgments are argued, not invented. And the final word belongs to the evidence.
